## The original claim

Sun et al. set out to find lasting transcriptional changes in the cells that
encode a fear memory in the mouse basolateral amygdala. TRAP2 mice express a
red reporter, tdTomato, in neurons that are active when tamoxifen is given, so
injecting it at memory recall labels the "engram" cells involved. The design
compared mice given fear training and later recall with three controls: mice
left in their home cage, mice that went through the procedure without the
shock, and mice that were shocked but never returned to the context for
recall. Single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics followed.

The headline results came from one small population: labelled inhibitory
neurons of the BLA.Int.Gpr88 subtype, compared between the fear-recall and
no-shock groups. The paper reported that *Tac1* fell more than sixfold and
*Penk* rose more than fourfold, and described a neuronal subpopulation defined
by increased *Penk* and decreased *Tac* expression as the most prominent
component of the engram. The figure legends state that significance was
assessed at unadjusted P < 0.05.

## Three statistical problems

Guan presented the critique by Mukamel and Yu as three separate errors, any one
of which inflates false discoveries.

**No correction for multiple testing.** Around 3,500 genes were tested. Even if
none truly differed, testing each at P < 0.05 would be expected to produce
roughly 180 "significant" genes. Mukamel and Yu reanalysed the data and found
no differentially expressed genes once a false discovery rate correction was
applied. The reply argued that correction risks overlooking genuine effects,
that whether to apply it depends on context, and that the analysis was meant
to generate hypotheses. Guan's response was that a hypothesis-generating
defence sits awkwardly with an abstract that presents memory-specific
transcriptional signatures as findings.

**Cells treated as independent replicates.** The comparison rests on 70 labelled
cells (45 fear-recall, 25 no-shock), drawn from only 11 mice (4 and 7). Cells
from the same animal share its genotype, history and processing, so treating
each cell as an independent sample overstates the evidence. The reply argued
that each labelling event during recall can be regarded as an independent
stochastic event. Guan's view was that even if activation is random, the
expression profiles of cells from one mouse are not independent. One attendee
proposed a simple way out: drop the p-values entirely. Pseudoreplication
distorts significance, but it does not change how genes rank by fold change.
The authors could have reported large-fold-change genes descriptively as
candidate markers. That framing would then require independent validation,
which the group did not find beyond agreement with the spatial data. Whether
the spatial and single-cell measurements came from the same animals, which
would limit how independent that agreement is, was not settled at the meeting.

**Double dipping.** The reply said the test had been applied to 56 genes
selected by systematic criteria, and that those genes replicated. The selection
included a large fold change between the same two groups, computed from the same
data, before testing those genes for a difference. This is selective inference
without the correction it requires. Under the null hypothesis a valid p-value
is uniformly distributed. Once genes have been filtered for apparent
differences in the same data, their p-values pile up near zero whether or not
any real effect exists. Guan illustrated this with simulations in which both
unadjusted testing and fold-change prefiltering pushed the actual false
discovery proportion well above the nominal level. Jiang et al. show the same
pattern in the real data. The 56 preselected genes have p-values concentrated
near zero, and standard multiple-testing corrections no longer behave as
intended on them.

Guan suggested what a sound version of the study would need: more mice,
because the current data lack power for the conclusions drawn; and, if genes
are to be preselected, a separate cohort to select them from. The four-group
design also prompted a constructive idea. The controls are currently used
informally during gene filtering. Guan proposed testing them formally, either
with conjunction p-values across contrasts, or with a regression model whose
interaction term isolates the effect of fear and recall together.

## Looking at variance instead of the mean

Jiang et al. accept the critique and then ask a different question. Their
reanalysis confirms that no gene shows a difference in mean expression after
correction, whether tested on pseudobulk profiles (one per mouse) or on single
cells. The top-ranked genes, without any correction, are enriched only for
general cellular functions such as RNA processing. However, several genes from
the original paper, *Tac1* among them, have distributions that differ in shape
between conditions, with little change in the mean.

They therefore tested for differential variability: whether the spread of a
gene's expression across cells differs between groups. Using Levene's test,
which compares deviations from the group centre and does not assume equal
variances, they report 169 genes at a 5% false discovery rate, including *Tac1*
and *Ramp1*. The top-ranked genes by this measure are enriched for terms such as
dendritic spine organisation and long-term memory. The pattern held after
removing extreme values, held when leaving out each mouse in turn, and did not
appear when cells were permuted between groups. The authors present this as a
partial reconciliation of the debate. The statistical criticisms stand, but the
genes Sun et al. highlighted may carry a real signal along a different axis.

Guan noted that variability is not independent of the mean. Under a negative
binomial model, the variance of a count grows with its mean. The Wilcoxon test
used for the original differential expression analysis compares ranks, and
can respond to differences in distribution shape as well as location. Separating
a change in variability from a change in mean is less clean than the contrast
between the two analyses suggests.

## Does the variability signal survive the same criticism?

One attendee argued that the biology favours this approach. Only a subset of
labelled neurons may change expression after recall. If so, an effect should
appear as a wider distribution in the fear-recall group rather than a uniform
shift, which a test of means will tend to miss. Some of the plotted genes
appeared bimodal, consistent with elevated expression in only some cells.

The sharper objection was that the variability test is also run on cells, not
mice. Levene's test cannot take mouse as a covariate in the way a generalised
linear model can. Jiang et al. justify the cell-level test on two grounds. Most
mice contribute too few cells to estimate a variance per mouse. And variance
ratios computed from pooled cells agree closely with those from mouse-level
pseudobulk. The group was not persuaded that this settles the matter. Agreement
of point estimates says nothing about whether the p-values are calibrated when
cells within a mouse are correlated. Guan agreed that the issue is tricky, and
suggested that a method decomposing variance into within-mouse and between-mouse
components would be the natural next step. Such a method would itself rest on
modelling assumptions. Asked whether a knockoff-based variable selection
approach could help, Guan noted that knockoffs assume independent samples, so
they would require pseudobulk data, and would likely have less power than a
standard differential expression test.

Two smaller questions stayed open. One attendee asked whether the unequal cell
numbers in the two groups could inflate the result; Levene's test accounts for
group size, but the imbalance is substantial. Another asked how many gene
ontology terms were enriched in total, since the figure shows a small set. Gene
ontology results are often unstable, and a figure showing selected terms leaves
open how representative they are. The same attendee was clear that the
differential variability analysis is a substantial improvement on the original.

Guan closed by placing the paper in a wider trend. Tests for differences in the
whole distribution of expression, not just its mean or variance, are becoming
computationally practical, and several tools now exist. A gene with no shift in
mean may still differ in variance, and one with neither may still differ in
shape. The broader lesson Guan drew was that a careful reanalysis can do more
than refute a claim: it can open a better-posed biological question.
